Top of mind: I mean, honestly? What’s top of mind is that we spent the whole quarter arguing about how we build with AI and never landed it. We shipped fine, the numbers held, but every Monday was the same conversation again and I walked into most weeks already tired of it.
Personal Best: The college tour with my daughter. I’d been putting it off two years. Four days, no laptop, and I didn’t open the fill-rate channel once, which for me is the whole achievement.
Professional Best: One rate card for the Gulf Coast markets. Sales and ops had been stuck on it for three quarters and we got it done in about six weeks, and nobody got rolled to do it. The offices stopped hearing two different prices from us, which was embarrassing.
Quarter Rating: Seven. Maybe six and a half, honestly.
Rating Reason: It was two quarters in one. Delivery side, we were good — fill rate held through the summer dip, the rate card landed, engineering shipped the worker app rewrite about when they said. That’s an eight. The other side is I sat in rooms all quarter talking about the same AI decision and we walked out of every one of them without making it, and that made me dread Mondays in a way I haven’t in six years. That’s a four. So the number is both of those, and I don’t want it to bury either one. If you read a seven and think we’re fine, you’ve missed the part that costs us next quarter, which is that nobody knows who decides.
EOS Example: The AI thing. Four conversations about what we build ourselves and what we buy, and every one ends with everybody nodding and nobody owning it. Then two weeks later somebody’s spun up a pilot anyway and we’re arguing about the same thing. It’s not a people problem, it’s that we never wrote it down, so everyone fills the gap with their own version.
Biggest Issue: Nobody can say who actually decides on AI. Six of us think we’re deciding it together, which means it doesn’t get decided. It’s been a month, maybe five weeks, since anybody moved on it.
Success Vision (90 days): The one I care about most is one fill-rate number and nobody walking in with a second one. That’s the whole first thing. Past that — a charter for how we build with AI, one page, boring, all six of us signed it, so when somebody spins up a pilot we point at the page instead of relitigating. The Gulf Coast group’s run a full quarter on the new rate card and we know whether it worked, actually know. GTM is down to one motion, so the single-office funnel is either fixed or it’s off. Engineering’s far enough through the worker app backlog that they’re asking us what’s next instead of us apologizing for the queue. And the thing I’d have stopped is the Monday leadership meeting where we update each other for ninety minutes and identify nothing. Half as long and twice as uncomfortable, I’d take that on its own.
Rock 1: First one is the number. One fill-rate number, one owner, read at the top of every L10, and nobody brings a spreadsheet to sit next to it.
Rock 1 — Why it matters: Because every argument we had last quarter started with two numbers. If we can’t agree what fill rate was, we can’t agree what moved it, and then we decide by whoever’s most certain that morning. That’s a bad way to run a marketplace.
Rock 1 — What done looks like: One dashboard, one written definition, one owner with their name on it. We’ve read it in the L10 every week of the quarter and nobody’s turned up with their own version. And when July’s question comes round again we answer it in the room.
Rock 1 — Who's involved: Ops owns it, data builds it, and me — I’m the one who has to stop accepting a second number.
Rock 2: Yeah. Collapse GTM to one motion. One play, written down, that every rep runs from lead to first filled shift.
Rock 2 — Why it matters: Two motions is where our handoffs die. Every seam is somewhere a new office waits a week on something, and offices don’t complain, they just stop posting shifts. It’s also the cheapest efficiency we’ve got — we don’t need more people, we need one path.
Rock 2 — What done looks like: The play’s on one page, every rep has run it end to end at least twice, and we can watch a lead go from marketing to a filled shift without anyone forwarding an email. And we’ve decided about the single-office funnel out loud, either way.
Rock 2 — Who's involved: Sales and marketing together, ops for the last mile, and me to make the call on the funnel.
Issues List: Oh — and the headcount conversation. Had it, not scheduled it. … Three or four. Who owns the AI decision. The single-office motion and whether we keep it. The headcount conversation before budget season. And if there’s room, how we run L10s now the room is twenty people.
